script:
[[CHAPTER Welcome]]

Welcome to Fernwick Nights. Tonight's story is The Bird That Stilled the Sea, a lesser-known tale from the Greek myths, told by Despina, who mends fishing nets on a harbor wall. Get comfortable, and listen to the water.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Word Halcyon]]

Sit here, on the upturned boat. The wood is still warm from the afternoon, and it smells of tar and salt. I will keep mending while I talk, if you do not mind. My hands never learned to stop. Now, here is what I want to ask you. Why does the old word halcyon mean calm days, and which small bird once made the whole winter sea hold still for her?

[pause]

You may have heard the word. Halcyon days: a stretch of gentle weather, a time when nothing is wrong. Sailors used it for centuries, and it comes from a Greek name. Alcyone. A woman, first, and then a bird. She is not one of the famous ones. Nobody carved her on a vase the way they did the great heroes. But the old poets kept her, and I think they were right to.

[pause]

Her father was Aeolus, keeper of the winds. Not the Aeolus with the bag of gales from the Odyssey, but a king of Thessaly, in the north, with the same name; the old tellers mixed them up, and so will I, once or twice. She married a man called Ceyx, who was a king too, the son of the Morning Star. By every account they were happy. They were the sort of couple who finish each other's sentences and get the ending wrong.

[long pause]

I should tell you where I am sitting, since you have been kind enough to sit with me. This is the old harbor wall, built of gray stone and white with salt at the top. Below us the small boats knock against each other, wood on wood, with a hollow, friendly sound. Someone is frying fish in a kitchen up the hill, and the smell of hot oil and lemon and oregano drifts down the steps. A bell tinkles on a goat somewhere. And the lantern beside my knee has begun to glow, a little orange circle on the stones.

[pause]

[[CHAPTER The Long Goodbye]]

Our story begins on a harbor very like this one. It is autumn, the water is the color of slate, and the air is full of the smell of rope and wet stone and woodsmoke from the houses above the quay. Ceyx is going on a voyage. Strange things have been happening in his land, and he wishes to ask for advice from a far-off place across the sea.

[pause]

Alcyone does not want him to go. She knows the sea. Her own father is the master of the winds, and she has seen what they can do. She holds his arm and begs him to stay, or at least to take her along. He cannot. So they stand on the quay together a long while, in the lamplight, and the ship's ropes creak, and the gulls complain.

[pause]

Ovid, the Roman poet who tells this best, says that she stood and watched the sails until they were a speck, and then a rumor, and then nothing. And then she went home and counted the nights. That is the part I like. Not the big tragedy. The counting.

[long pause]

I have done some counting myself, in my time. My husband fished these waters for forty years, and I would sit at the kitchen table with a cup of sage tea, listening for his boots on the stones. You learn the sound of one particular step in a hundred. Slow, a little dragging on the left. And you learn to put the kettle on a moment before you hear it. That is all I will say about that. He always came home.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Cave of Sleep]]

I will tell the hard part quickly, because it is hard, and you are here to rest. Out at sea, a wind came up from the south. The waves grew tall. A great one rolled over the ship, and that was the end of Ceyx's voyage. His long day was over. He said her name as he went, and the sea carried the sound away.

[pause]

At home, Alcyone knew nothing. She lit the lamps. She wove him a cloak to welcome him back. And the goddess Hera, who looked after wives, felt sorry for her and could not bear to watch her wait. So she called her rainbow messenger, Iris, and sent her to the House of Sleep.

[pause]

Iris came down along her own bright arc, trailing colors across the gray sky. She flew to the very edge of the world, to the land of the Cimmerians, where the sun never reaches. There is a cave there, in the side of a mountain. Poppies grow at its mouth, and other drowsy herbs, and their scent is sweet and a little dusty, like old honey. A river called Lethe slides past outside, and the sound of it makes everything drowsy.

[pause]

No rooster crows there. No dog barks. No branch creaks in the wind, because there is no wind. In the middle of the cave stands a great bed of ebony, with black curtains, and on it lies Sleep himself, Hypnos, with his limbs loose and his head on his arm. Around him lie his sons, the dreams, a thousand of them, like leaves on a forest floor.

[long pause]

Iris waved her hand to clear the heavy air, and the cave brightened with rainbow light. Sleep opened one eye. Then he lifted himself on one elbow, and nodded, and sank back. He was very slow about it. Ovid says he was almost undone by his own heavy eyelids. But he heard the request, and he chose his son Morpheus, who can wear any human shape and speak in any voice, to carry the message.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER Morpheus at the Window]]

Morpheus flew without a sound, on wings as soft as moths, and came to the room where Alcyone lay. He took the shape of Ceyx, pale and wet-haired, standing at the foot of her bed. He had her husband's face, and her husband's voice. "Do not wait for me any longer," he said. "The sea has kept me. Mourn me a little, and then let me go."

[pause]

She woke in the gray light before the dawn. The lamp had burned low, and the room was cold and still. She knew what she had been told. She put on her cloak and went down to the shore, to the very pier where she had said goodbye, and the tide was coming in, quiet and silver, with a faint foam at its edge.

[pause]

Far out on the water, something pale was drifting toward her. She stood and watched it come. And as she reached out her arms toward it, a change came over her. Her arms grew light. Feathers, soft and blue-green, spread along them. Her voice thinned to a small sweet cry, and she rose, over the water, over the foam, and went skimming out to meet him.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Seven Quiet Days]]

Ovid says that the gods pitied them both. Ceyx too was changed, and the two of them became kingfishers, bright little birds the color of sea glass and sunset. They lived together, and they were happy again, which is more than most stories give anyone.

[pause]

And here is the best part, the part that gave us the word. Kingfishers, the old people said, build their nests on the water, floating on the winter waves. Alcyone laid her eggs in midwinter, when the sea is at its roughest. But her father Aeolus remembered his daughter. Each year, the old writers say, he holds back the winds for seven days before the shortest day and seven days after it. The sea lies flat and glassy. The sky is pale. And the little bird broods in peace on her nest of fishbones, rocking gently.

[long pause]

It is a pretty picture, and the old writers loved it. They imagined the nest like a little round ball, woven from the spines of fish, floating on the swell like a cork. The mother bird sits on it, and the water lifts and lowers her, lifts and lowers, as slowly as a cradle. Her feathers are the blue of a deep pool in the shade, and the orange of embers on her breast. Soft, warm, and quite safe. She looks out at the flat sea, and the sea looks back, and nothing at all is the matter.

[long pause]

Those are the halcyon days. The Greeks believed in them, and so did the Romans, and in some harbors the fishermen will still tell you that the weather turns kind for a week in the deep of winter. Whether the weather agrees, I could not say. But I have stood on this wall on a flat gray December morning, with the sea like a sheet of tin, and I have seen a small blue flash dive from the post beside me. I do not ask questions.

[long pause]

Real kingfishers, I am told, do not nest on water at all. They dig holes in riverbanks. But I have never minded that. A myth does not need to be right about birds. It is right about something else: that waiting is a kind of love, and that the world, now and then, bends a little to meet it.

[long pause]

The light on the water is going now. The tide slides in and out below us. The net is nearly done. You can hear how slowly the waves come, one, and a long wait, and another. The little bird rocks on her nest, and the sea holds still for her.

[long pause]

[[SECOND]]

[[CHAPTER Once More, Slowly]]

Why does halcyon mean calm days? Because of a small bird, and a king's daughter who waited.

[pause]

Alcyone watched her husband's ship go. She lit the lamps. She counted the nights.

[long pause]

Sleep sent a dream with his face. She went to the shore at dawn. And she was changed into a bird, light and blue, and flew out to the water to find him.

[pause]

Now every winter, her father stills the winds. Seven days before the shortest day, and seven days after. The sea lies flat. The little bird rests on her floating nest.

[long pause]

And that is the story of the halcyon days. The boat is warm, and the net can wait, and you are welcome to stay as long as the sea is quiet. Good night.
